newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower after brief rise on CPI.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower after brief rise on CPI.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Wednesday after erasing a brief, early spike up on news that prices at the retail level barely rose in January.

Near the start of the day's trading session, the Labor Department reported that its Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose just 0.1 percent in January, the smallest monthly increase since last summer. The CPI rose 0.3 percent in December.
With its more volatile food and energy components deleted, the so-called core CPI also rose just 0.1 percent. Both were even more benign inflation readings than had been forecast.
U.S. Treasury prices rallied on the news, but the gains were fleeting.

"I think what happened is that a minute after the report came out, the typical domestic trader said, 'Inflation can't get any better than this; it's time to take some profits,'" said Carey Leahey, senior vice president and senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.

While the Labor Department reported the January CPI data, the Commerce Department reported that the U.S. trade deficit widened 29.6 percent to $10.29 billion in December, versus a revised $7.94 billion trade gap in November.

"Overseas investors might have taken their cue from the wider trade deficit, seeing it as potentially leading to a weaker dollar down the road," Leahey explained. "These were the two influences that sent bond prices lower."

The 6.50-percent February 2027 30-year Treasury bond, up more than a quarter of a point immediately after the CPI report, spent the afternoon drifting at lower levels. In late trade, it sank a bit lower still, ending at 100-19/32, its yield at 6.58 percent, versus 6.55 percent at Tuesday's close.
"The CPI was excellent," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
"But the market seemed to be saying that the news can't get any better than this, which is another way of saying that the best news is behind us," he said.
While the Federal Reserve is on hold in terms of adjusting monetary policy, the economy continues to run at a pace that has caused the labor markets to get very tight, said Williams.
"As a result, some gradual pickup in inflation this spring still seems inevitable, especially from these very low levels," he said.
Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc., sounded a similar theme.

"Everything on the CPI front looks outstanding," said Lieberman. "But from an analytical view, because the labor market continues to be fairly tight and job growth continues to remain quite strong, the sheer momentum of the economy insures that the labor market will tighten up further.
"At some point, that should translate into higher prices, but it's very difficult to see whether that will show up sooner or later," said Lieberman.
News of the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping saw the dollar spike up briefly in mid-afternoon and bond prices briefly come off their lows.
Lieberman said the news had only a minor impact on the markets because Deng had been ill for a long time.

"There's been recurring speculation as to how the political system in China will handle succession. In some sense, they have already done so," said Lieberman. "With his death, perhaps the political situation in China will become more dynamic. It's hard to say. But no one was caught off guard by Deng's death and no one has a better answer today than they did yesterday as to how things will shake out."

At the close, the three-month Treasury bill rate was down three basis points to 4.96 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.03 percent. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.17 percent.

Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-4/32, yielding 5.80 percent, the five-year note ended down 5/32 at 100-19/32, yielding 6.11 percent. Ten-year notes fell 8/32 to 99-17/32, yielding 6.31 percent. (( -- 212-859-1679 ))
